review_headline: Solid overall with a slow UI, and yes, of course the AI cheats.
review_body:
I'll get to the AI in a minute. First, a few points about other aspects of the game:

· Overall, the game is enjoyable, once you realize what you're dealing with and set your game plan accordingly. The graphics are good, the presentation is professional, and EA have kept the UI simple and mostly intuitive without sacrificing any of the core, classic game play of the board game.

· Once you've played the game a couple of times, you're going to want things to move along a lot faster than they do. Having to wait for the dice to roll, for the little pieces to move around the board, for the thought bubbles to animate during the auction phase, for the visual effect of a colorful flash when a monopoly is acquired -- all of this becomes tiresome quickly. Of course, you can speed things up by holding the fast forward button superimposed over the right side of the screen, but you've got to keep your finger there and as soon as you let go to touch some other control, it's back to regular speed, which is a problem since the FF button appears available only *after* one of the slowest parts of the game, i.e. the dice roll. There definitely needs to be an option to accelerate the game by default.

· The game offers no means of retaining preferences. It doesn't remember how many opponents you played last time, it doesn't remember the AI level you selected, it doesn't remember which table you chose, it doesn't even remember which language you picked (though this could be a problem in the case of giving your phone to someone who didn't speak your language, but how often is that going to happen, and you can just re-install the game, anyway). Weak and annoying.

· It would be nice to see EA provide some paid DLC for this title. Extra playing pieces, aesthetically different boards (e.g. the Lord of the Rings version that came out a few years back), boards with geometry on the periphery of the properties representing their character (e.g. projects for Baltic, penthouses for Park Place), animating the pieces according to what befalls them on change/CC squares, etc.

OK now, the AI:

First of all, yes the game cheats, absolutely. Look people, give yourselves some credit; this game doesn't have Houdini- or Shredder-level intelligence, so on even the highest of the three AI levels, you're going to figure out a very effective strategy quickly and get bored as a result if it doesn't rig the game. This is a $5 title on a small handheld device; EA aren't going to put some egghead with a masters in neural networking who makes a $200K+ salary onto this project. The dice can be mercilessly favoritist at times, sure, but knowing that this is the case should help you shape your game plan.

Apart from the jacked dice, the first thing to realize when you are playing this game is that when you are playing versus multiple AI opponents, you are not battling two or three guys with their own individual interests. What is actually happening is that you are battling players who are in collusion against you. They have little concern for their own prosperity; as long as they take you out, they're happy. This is generally how they'll play, and for evidence of this, you need look no further than the fact that an opponent will make ruinous, totally foolhardy trades with another AI opponent if it gives the latter a monopoly. So basically, come at the game knowing that you are essentially battling just one other player who gets two or three extra turns in a row every time (more if either AI opponent rolls doubles, of course).

I've got about an 80% success rate at soundly defeating the game on level 3 AI with three opponents. My top priorities, in order, are:

1. Put my finger into everybody's pie, i.e. do my level best not to allow any opponent to secure a monopoly that isn't a utility or the brown properties. Of course, this often involves purchasing properties fromAI players at a significantly increased price (e.g. I usually have to spend $290 to $300 to buy an orange square from the computer), but in the long run it is totally worth it and you can always mortgage these properties for some extra cash. If I can block monopolies on brown, that's nice of course, but it isn't crucial, since the most those properties pay out is $450 (which shouldn't be a big deal later in the game). On level 3 AI, the most I've had at the end of the game is a little over $13,000. ( miloonline.net / misc / monopoly_screenshot.png -- remove spaces in URL.)

2. Make a point of acquiring at least three railroads, and try to monopolize the orange squares. This is just basic monopoly strategy; railroads are cash cows when you've got three or (especially) all of them, and the orange squares are the most frequently landed upon properties (thanks to jail); although you will see the computer landing with conspicuous frequency on the CC space between St. James and Tennessee, or curiously rolling 10s, 11s, and 12s coming away from jail/just visiting, the likelihood that the AI will eventually hit these properties is still good relative to all the rest.

3. One property on all colors but orange is generally enough. Remember, priority one is blocking monopolies. If you don't do that, you are very likely in for a world of hurt, thanks to the AI collusion and the laughable dice rolls. Obviously, if you can get multiple colors in a non-orange zone without making yourself strapped for cash (i.e. less than $200 early on, less than $500 in mid-game), then go for it (see point 5), but don't overextend yourself by purchasing properties in non-orange zones where you already have property.

4. When you land on a non-orange color in which you already own property, start an auction then bid high just to force the AI to shell out for it. You have to get a feel for this, based mostly on how the AI players are bidding in each individual case. It isn't uncommon for the computer to pay 50% or more of the default price for the last available property in a zone in which you own at least one square.

5. *If you can spare the cash*, i.e. if you can spend money and stay on track with objectives 1 and 2, then buy more than one property in a zone just to get some trading power without having to risk giving the computer a monopoly. A lot of times, the computer will not sell you a property even if offered 500% or more of list price, because it doesn't want to give you the power that would come of the acquisition. However, the computer almost always *will* trade for property. (Sometimes, when things aren't exactly going swimmingly, I'll even risk trading a property the color of which still has one or two unpurchased squares, in the hope that I'll be able to build up myself with the trade before the last one or two unclaimed properties get bought. This is often a chance worth taking if you're having trouble meeting objectives 1 and 2.)

6. (Related to 5) Always buy utilities. Previously, I never bought utilities (which is usually a good strategy when you're playing against human opponents -- their return on investment stinks), but just like real life, no merchandise has intrinsic value. For some reason, the AI fairly highly values utilities, so you can use them in high-value trades even though they don't cost much to acquire.

7. Unless none of your opponents has nor can possibly acquire a monopoly, or unless all of them are severely hurting for cash -- or unless you are simply way ahead of everyone else and therefore cash drunk -- never build hotels. Just build three or four houses on each property (whichever you can afford), with the aim of causing a housing shortage. Again, basic strategy.

8. Pretty much never accept a trade initiated by the computer. The AI trading logic is bizarre, 99% of the time I just immediately wave off the trade, sort of like a fly buzzing into my ear. You want *what* for *what*? LOL GTFO

I may be overlooking a few points, but I'm pretty sure that these are my main plans of attack. Of course, more of the standard tactics certainly apply; pay to get out of jail early on and happily stay in jail later on, prefer building on the second properties of a row to the first properties (more return on investment) except for red/yellow, never stop at two houses (rent shoots way up at three houses), don't bother with green monopolies (statistically low visitation rates), etc.

Overall, I'm quite satisfied with this handheld version of Monopoly (which I played back in my iPhone days, also). There are still times when the loaded dice cause me to roll my eyes and curse aloud, or even to chuckle somewhat madly with disbelief -- observe what happens if you get a monopoly very early on (usually, you'll find the AI pieces somewhat frantically and miraculously landing on unsold properties, and quickly trading among themselves) -- but as they say, knowing is half the battle. A cheater is no fun, but a predictable cheater can be dealt with. review_headline: FINALLY a sync program that works...FAST
review_body:
I have tried to use Songbird, Doubletwist and HTC Sync to sync my music to my HTC Evo. Songbird would take for-ev-er to mount the SD card, Doubletwist recopied all my songs every time and HTC sync took five minutes to update the library and then at least an hour and a half to sync playlists and then copy songs. I could find no program that seemed to sync as quickly and accurately as iTunes synced my iPod Touch. Now I have.

I'm using iSyncr for both my HTC Evo phone and my Acer Iconia tablet. I had trouble with a couple of songs the first couple of times I tried to sync, but once I unchecked those and ran one full sync (about 4500 songs) they synced fine the second time. Of course the first sync took a long time since the songs had to be copied fully. What has amazed me is how iSyncr performs on subsequent syncs. It seems to sync only what has changed and gets the sync over and done with. I can now sync whenever I want - I don't have to set aside time to make sure the sync happens. I can sync and go - just like iTunes works with my iPod Touch.

To the developer: THANK YOU.

review_headline: Would be better with some tweaks.....
review_body: Playing a round in the timed mode is annoying.  You are basically cut off from doing your best, even if you can recognize and swipe words without taking time to think.  This is because as the timer goes down, the speed at which the balls replenish becomes so fast that it's virtually impossible to make any more words and get more points.  I can understand the speed being increased, but not to a point where it's so fast that 1) it's basically telling you that the game is over no matter how fast you can swipe, and 2) when it's going that fast, it doesn't recognize any words you DO manage to get in at the last second if it's filling up the bottom row.  This happens every single time that the time is about to run out and the last 5 or 6 balls are flying in -- any word you swipe anywhere on the board doesn't register at all.  Like I said, I don't mind it going faster toward the end, but not so fast where you can't make words or get points for anything before the clock has stopped.  The timed game needs to be a little longer, that's all.  Playing a round in the relaxed mode gives you the ability to control the speed at which the balls appear on the screen, and is a much better gameplay.  At a medium speed, you can go 5 hours without it stopping, and gain a tremendous number of points, if you have the ability.  However, the complaint is that I feel it's going a little faster on the bottom half of the screen.  The problem with this is that the game then forces you to make little words on the first couple of rows and makes you not want to wait for 4 or 5 rows to fill up to be able to create bigger words and gain more points.  It's as if the gameplay then becomes less of a \\"make a big word, gain more points\\" game and more of a \\"make any word as fast as you can, as small as you can, and just get rid of the damn letters as fast as you can\\" game.  It's really a hassle to play once the screen becomes just half full.  By the time you quickly scan the board to visualize your word, another row has just filled up, and you're not concentrating on the words but just on the fact that you have to clear that screen.  That's why this game would be more enjoyable for those looking for the excitement of clearing a board as fast as possible, arcade style, and not for those who like \\"word games\\" because of the intellectual challenge.  If this app wants to combine both, they need to ease up on the rate at which the balls are replenished because the scale is tipped in the direction of speed and not in the direction of \\"content,\\" which is more important to fans of word games.  If not, this game may as well just get rid of the letters altogether and go with colored ball strings and become another bejeweled clone, because that's what's it's like now without the improvements to the \\"create the best word you can\\" aspect of the game.

review_headline: Robust note-taking app that DOES backup
review_body: I started using ColorNotes several months ago on my mobile, and it was among the first apps I looked for when I got a Kindle Fire.  It's a very easy app to set up, you decide whether you want to create essentially a text document or a checklist, then type in what you want to save, just like other note-taking apps. Copying/pasting from other docs works well, too, though you can't turn a text doc into a checklist, or at least I haven't figured that one out yet.  (If I do, I'll add that to this review.)  One can even color-code their notes, as well as name those categories (such as naming the green notes "household"), and organize notes by those categories or in simple alpha order.  Some reviewers mentioned the inability to save notes.  Really?  ColorNote offers an online backup to their cloud, which you can set up to sync your notes manually or every time you open the app.  Don't trust their cloud?  Then you can use your backup app (you do have a backup app, right?) to backup your notes to your device or SD card or to the backup app's server.  Don't use a backup app?  Then save individual notes to your SD card.  Or after saving to SD, you can plug your device into your computer and copy the notes over for even more backing up.  And if none of those options sound appealing, use their Send feature to copy to the clipboard and paste into another doc, send as an attachment, email it to yourself or someone else, send via Bluetooth, or post it to Facebook.  There's also a feature called Archive that I suspect backs up the notes in a different manner, but I have not used it so can't say for certain if that is yet another way to save your notes.  But including Archive, that's THIRTEEN ways and places you can backup all that data you entered.  And if those features aren't enough for you, you can also password-protect any or all of your notes.  Use the built-in calendar to send yourself a reminder to do whatever you typed into a certain note.  Run a search of all yournotes for a word or phrase.  Use their online-sync feature to always have your most up-to-date notes sync between the devices you use the app on -- for me that syncs my notes on my mobile and my Fire so there's no need to figure out which is the "correct" version.  Each time I've thought of something I'd like to organize and look around for apps to do it, most if which cost a few bucks, I realize that my trusty ColorNotes will do the same thing.  I'd happily pay money for all this but the developer is generous enough to provide all of this FOR FREE.  Seriously.  You might find all these features in some other app, but you're already looking into this one so just go ahead and press that download button, I'm sure you'll be pleased.

It's pretty obvious what this company's model is. Get parents to get this game for their children (there are *tons* of parents who do this sort of thing). They hand a device to their kids who then charge a couple hundred for-real-type dollars. Parents can't get money back, Glu laughs their way to the bank, kids are none the wiser.

General caveat for parents with ANY game you're getting for your kids: play it a little first - see if the game is trying to leverage your children's naivete to profit (can they download other paid games? are there in-game purchases they could make? are there questionable ads that are placed for little fingers to click on that may take them to unsavory sites?) - these companies are downright scary and it makes me sad that Amazon would feature stuff like this on their Kindle Fire apps main page. Where's the customer-centricity in that Amazon? Or is the 30% of the in-app purchases too tempting to put the customer first?

product_title: puz-ZEN-le Zen Puzzle Game Relaxation App
review_headline: A nice concept, but it needs some tweaking
review_body:
NOTE: I played puz-ZEN-le Zen on my Kindle Fire.

I like the concept for puz-ZEN-le Zen. It's a video version similar to the old pencil-and-paper brainteasers where you have to draw straight lines connecting objects, with every object required to be covered, and a limit on the number of lines. In this case, you're limited to four lines, which are set by pulling four nodes into place.

It's very simple to play, but the higher levels get progressively more challenging. I would give the puzzle four or five stars, except for a couple of details that need improvement.

* The lines crossing the flowers must cross the exact center of each flower for the flower to light up. There's almost no tolerance for error, so it's difficult to line up the nodes. Even lifting your finger off the screen can shift a node a tiny bit and miss a flower's center. This became frustrating after a while.

* I expected some relaxing zen-like background music, as in games like Quell, but there was none. Instead, there are three buttons which when pressed, create some gong or bell sounds, but only if you keep pressing them.

So, overall, a very nice concept that could have been executed much better.

My wife spotted Pinball HD when she was looking for some new games for her Kindle Fire, and she told me I should check it out.

Seeing as mobile games come in at under a few bucks a pop, I generally am willing to download just about anything to give it a try if it even looks remotely decent.

Pinball HD definitely looked decent. So I figured what the heck.

Upon starting to play, it quickly became evident that this is the real deal pinball simulator. It controls very well, and I love how the ball definitely feels like a real ball...basically, the physics of it seem to be just about spot on. I have yet to encounter anything in my play time that made me think \\"wait a minute, a ball wouldn't do that in real life.\\"

It's very easy to play. You simply tap on the side of the screen that you want to use the flipper on, and the flipper moves.

The graphics are top notch, and so are the sound effects. It looks simply amazing on the Kindle Fire.

The production values are also very high. You get a great virtual tour of the board, but oddly, it happens AFTER you play the board. The menu is pretty bare bones, but it works just fine and lets you easily pick which machine you want to play.

If there is ANY downside at all to this game it would be the fact that there are only three machines available at the start. For the price, however, I simply can't justify letting this actually affect my opinion of the game. I would like to see more tables available in the future, and I would gladly pay for them to add into this app.

Overall, a very high quality app at a very appealing price.

review_headline: OMG!  I feel like I'm home again!

I did not know about this app or I would have gotten months ago!

I have really missed my Palm and Graffiti... I have not gotten the hang of typing on a virtual keyboard or Swyping successfully. I so often do not write what I meant to and then the mis-written word is in the Swype dictionary to keep coming up in the future. I know I can delete a word, but who has time for it when you are trying to write a text or a search term or whatever? So when I opened my Amazon Free App of the Day this morning, I was so happily surprised! I was so fast using Graffiti on my Palm and now I can get up to speed again! I don't know why others have said that the word prediction is not so good. For me, it is a great improvement over the Graffiti on my Palm, and it is very accurate and quick!

For those who have not had a Palm and used Graffiti, it may be pretty hard to start. I could not find a good video tutorial. I bought my Palm at the Franklin Covey store years ago, and got a lot of training and support there. But Franklin Covey is now extinct, because of technology taking over from planner notebooks. But I digress. I love having Graffiti once again and want to say to Access and Amazon--THANK YOU SO VERY MUCH FOR THIS WONDERFUL GIFT! I would have paid for it, had I known it was there. $3 for this app is well worth it, and you can try it out the free version first to see if you like it and can master it.

review_headline: Charming and beautiful introduction to The Nutcracker
review_body: This app is lovely - part children's book, part art collection, part advent calendar.  The really wonderful thing about the app is that every page was painted by Yoko Tanaka, one of my favorite painters and children's book illustrators.  She was the artist who illustrated [[ASIN:0763652989 The Magician's Elephant]] and [[ASIN:B00375LN6A Sparrow Girl]].  Having her work in this format is wonderful.    On top of the beautifully animated paintings, every piece of music from the Nutcracker Suite accompanies the images.  There are 26 or 27 total pieces of music (one for each page, as well as a couple more for the Menu Page and Credits/Title screens.  My only complaint is that it would be nice to be able to gift the app, since it is holiday-themed.

It's a great game if you can get it to work.  I like it because the cards are large, colourful, easy to see, close together and the drag and drop is snappy and responsive. I also enjoy the \\"collecting\\" aspect that allows you to purchase new card backs and backgrounds from your in-game winnings. So you don't need to use any real money at all if you don't want. - Although you can purchase card backs/backgrounds with real money if you want. The only thing that would improve the game would be if they added more stuff to the ingame store. If you play it a lot, you will pretty much have everything unlocked in a short time.

It's a simple, cute story that preschool/kindergarten/first grade kids should enjoy. It's a short illustrated, interactive story that should hold kids' attention long enough to finish. The story encourages kids to touch and swipe the screen to make objects move or do some other action, such as lights flashing. There are also sound effects. product_title: The Mystery of the Crystal Portal (Full)
review_body: [[ASIN:B001KC03UE The Mystery of the Crystal Portal [Download]]]  When I first started using this game, I noted that it was a lovely game.  It has stunning graphics of Japan, the Swiss Alps, Mexico, and Russia.  For a game, it is nicely done.  As one travels to these lands, you find objects (it's a hidden object game) and find tokens that piece together to let you enter new places.  It is nice.  However, my one proviso is that is is very short-lived.  I zipped through the different lands and levels in a day.  I started on it last night and toyed with it this morning and by 9 am it was done.  Done!  I expected to go to another level..see a different view of the same lands with new objects. Nothing. Done.  If you want more, you have to run through the same scenarios again...exactly.  It was not a free app; it was not 99 cents, it was $5.  Ok, that's not a lot of money but still, one night for the whole thing?    Having said that, it is a nice little game with gorgeous graphics, very classily done.  Sandy

This seems to have all the same features as that version including, apparently, the same numeric identities for each of the possible deals (very useful if you are pleasing the deals methodically to avoid repetition).  Gameplay is smooth and it has an excellent autocomplete which offers to  take over once you have freed all of the cards from being the possibility of being trapped by a higher-numbered card.  It is best played in landscape mode as the cards can be difficult to select with one's finger of the cards are too small. review_headline: Love the app, a few suggestions
review_body: I just started the couch to 5k routine last week, and was looking for a decent app to help track my progress.  Since this app was free for a day, I figured I'd give it a shot, nothing to loose.  I've only used it once so far, but I love it!  The audio notifications are great, you don't have to keep looking at the screen, and it works even if you have music playing.  I do have a few suggestions though:  1  Needs an option to fast-forward through a workout.  While running, I accidentaly hit stop, and had no way of restarting the routine without going back to the beginning.  2  Music integration is good, but would be better if you could pick the music player (Pandora, AudioGalaxy)  3  Built in GPS capability would be nice, so I could track the distance I've ran.  Using this app, a music player, and an app to track my distance ([[ASIN:B004VFJMYK Cardio Trainer Pro]]) is tough on my phone!  All in all, I'm pleased with this app, and fully recommend it, either free for a day or the regular full price.

It was bound to happen - free IP calling for cell phones! With GrooVe IP, as long as there is a strong data signal (or open wireless connection), calls are free!  I use this on T-Mobile and works great. Call quality is just about as good as the regular network. What does this mean for wireless carriers? Maybe the beginning of the decline. Eventually all you'll need is a data network with VOIP. Tradition voice network will be obsolete. How soon will this happen and will the carriers - Verizon, AT&T, Sprint and T-Mobile pull their strings to kill VOIP? They will surely try, but eventually will lose. Long live VOIP on wireless devices!

review_headline: Good tool to have on your device
review_body: I have used andie graph with TI83 and TI86 roms and it is good. Added benefit is its free. But its complicated to use for a first time user like me. We used non graphing calculators like scientific casio's (basic) where I come from. I purchased this application as I am brushing up on my calculus studies. I found the TI difficult to use and also its graphing seems to be pretty basic.\nThe mathpac+ handles upto 9 single variable functions for graphing, derivation, integration etc at a single go. Visually it looks good and adds more interest. The area of the graph between x axis and curve i.e. integration within specified limits is calculated and shown on the graph. Right now the graphs that are plotted deal with y as a function of x and hence only area can be found via integration. What would be really cool is if graphs can be plotted in 3 dimensions ie. z as a function of y and x. That would immeasurably increase the value of this program but I guess I am asking for too much. The maxima and minima derived are shown within the specified limits on the graph. These graphs can be saved as snapshot in your photo gallery as a fullscreen image (although the file name was not the same that I entered while saving the snapshot, a bit of a bug). I guess all this is achieved for free on the TI without the fancy graphing abilities. However using this is a breeze compared to the TI's. So if your familiar with the TI, $10 (let alone $20 that this app normally costs) may seem a bit steep especially since there are free graphing apps out there but I don't think they do further operations like integration\/differentiation on graphed functions. I felt so to initially, but then I explored the matrix lists and matrix calculations. It supports user specified matrices (I went as high as a 16x16, entering all the values was a pain). It carried out the calculations like inverse, transpose, addition, multiplication etc without issues. One side note is that actually saving the 16x16 matrix took time. The app hung for around 15secs and I was asked whether I wanted to force close the app by android. I declined and gave the app some more time after which it came back to life. I suppose handling a 16x16 list is processor intensive. Other than this the maths part of the app has all the basic trignometric, logarithmic and other scientific functions that any self respecting scientific calculator app will do. It also supports permutations and combinations which is good. If you still feel the price is too high then mathpac+ also comes with a host of statistical tools like regressions, F test, One-sample Z test\/intervals, distributions which I know nothing of but its good to know that I have tools in my mobile device if I need them some day. Again the data is stored in lists which can be saved. The person who is actually developing this app has a good video tutorial website which one can check out to see if this is the kind of app they are looking for. It will show what this app can do much better.\nThis app may be invaluable to a statistician who needs it and right now just about makes the grade for a maths student at the $10 price. All I will say is if you can afford it go for it else purely from the math point you can stick with the TI emulators or the multitude of free scientific calculators and graphing tools. The major plus is this has all the tools available in a single package besides offering additional functionality not present in anything on market.

review_headline: Nope: as likely to crash your PC as synch your tunes...
review_body:
18 month update: you can read the rest of the review if you want: but you don't have to as long as you remember one word: AVOID.

My 18-month history with this app is that it is fine as a player, but fails badly at during the wireless synching process. Primary issues (which are chronic):
-\\"sync fail\\" error message as the first reponse to a request to synch with your local media content.
-frequent --and complete-- locking up the Windows machine its working with during sync attempts.
-after synching, leaves duplicate versions of tracks (I ended up with 999 duplicate tracks before deleting this beast!

If you're like me, and simply won't become an iPhone convert (because everybody knows that iTunes-iPhone synching is instant and painless!) try something else instead (like [[ASIN:B004O9DEI8 Winamp]]...which immediately recognized and removed doubleTwist's multiple song residue.

----
One month update: reducing to four stars for the following unstable behavior (applies to the desktop component, NOT the one installed on the smartphone):

-While updating the songs libary in the doubleTwist desktop client (which essentially syncs doubleTwist with iTunes), doubleTwist froze...completely freezing a very stable installation of Windows 7 Professional with it. This is the first application to ever do this on a rock solid Windows desktop. I was forced to power down and restart using the desktop power switch.

-After restart, doubleTwist would not launch.

-A review of doubleTwist user forums suggested a removal/reinstall.

-After removal/reinstall, doubleTwist still would not launch.

-Further exploration of its user forums suggested removing the associated user data in the Windows AppData folder. I did this, followed by a second uninstall/reinstall. Note: Although power users of Windows will be comfortable doing this, this folder is hidden by default, and many users won't enjoy the same comfort.

-After removing the AppData user information and the second reinstall, doubleTwist launched, and re-synced with iTunes and the phone again, but:

I have a fundamental mistrust of applications that not only freeze, but extend that behavior to the operating system.

Leaving this at four stars for now: but if it happens again, it's one star...and off my system!

Original review is below:

..but for about the cost of one trip to a a high-end coffee shop, this app is worth it.

Once you decide that your path to smart phone use is going to be outside of the iPhone domain, you've already signed yourself up for a little extra work in getting good synchronization between your phone and the data you want to make portable by placing it on your phone...seamless integration between the iPhone and iTunes is one of the areas where Apple products are best.

Before purchasing this app, I used the free version (requires USB connection, has ads and is not offered by Amazon..but 'Droid users know where to get it) to synch my desktop iTunes music collection to an [[ASIN:B003N9B3CY HTC EVO 4G Android Phone]] and it worked just fine. I already manage/synch an [[ASIN:B002L6HDPG iPod nano 5G]] via a USB connector, and the free, wired solution was is perfectly functional one for synching your iTunes (or Windows Media Player) library to a smart phone.

But sometimes you literally want to cut the cord, and doubleTwist AirSync does this very well. Upgrading and installing the paid AirSync version was fast and painless. After connecting the Evo to my wireless network and entering a pairing passcode into the desktop client --a one-time process--, re-synch of the doubleTwist music directory was complete in less than a minute. Obviously, synching full libraries for the first time will take much longer. In fact I'd recommend the free/wired option for for your first synch simply because of the faster data transfer rates with a wired connection.

Trips to the desktop/laptop are now thing of the past for digital media file management (it works with tunes, videos and images) on your smart phone. What's not to like ?mply because of the faster data transfer rates with a wired connection.

review_headline: Never won at chess so much in my life
review_body:
Test devices:
Samsung Epic, Android 2.2 official
Viewsonic gTablet, Calkulin+Clemsyn 1.5ghz Froyo Combo V6

Normally, I lose at chess all the time. And in this game, that's the idea. It plays mostly like chess, in that all the pieces all move the same, but exactly. Taking the king, or having your taken, does not end the game. The game only ends when one player is wiped out or can't move. If you have a move that will take a piece, you must take it, just as in some variants of Checkers. Given my history of playing chess, I thought Losing Chess would be right up my alley. Not so! Losing is hard in this game! Quite a challenge!

Visually, Losing Chess is in right in the \\"ok\\" range. Not great but not ugly. Sadly, it doesn't scale up on the gTablet, instead hiding out in one corner. No sound effects, music, or other audio fanfare. Moves are wicked fast, leaving you to look around to see which piece your opponent moved and where. There are multiple difficulty levels to choose from, giving you better challenges to your losing skills.

I hope you found this review helpful, and if not, feel free to leave comments/questions.

(I mean, I make fun of elves all the time, being treehugging flippy-wristed nature loving hippies, and all.) Maybe if it were a different kind of game, or if they'd spread the love to other political \\"sides\\", or not been so heavy-handed with it... But it just came off as \\"mean\\". I didn't expect it from this kind of game and it rubbed me the wrong way.

2) The last level was way too difficult. I wasn't the only one who had a problem with it, according to several forums and websites. I tried it on Normal multiple times with various strategies, and finally beat it on Easy by ***Spoiler:::[REDACTED]*** Heh! You thought I was going to tell you.

I originally bought my Samsung Tablet as a travel companion and replacement for my Garmin GPS and it incredibly outdated information.  While the actual on the road functionality of the Google Navigation is far superior to that of Garmin - Google Navigation falls way short in the trip planning area.  There is no native route building or way-point management.  Logic would dictate that you could build a route in either Google Earth or Google Maps and then load it into Google Navigation.  This is not the case.  Oddly, Google Earth does have the native functionality to export a route to Garmin or TomTom, but not Google Navigation.  BestRoute allows you to build a route.  It then pushes it into Google Navigation.  It apears to actually load the route and then switch over to Google Navigation; but it does this without the user having to take any action.      Routes can be created either from inside the app or by importing a KML file from Google Earth.  While the information about the app does indicate that the import function is available, the documentation/instructions does not actually explain how this is done. I was able to figure it out and I was very pleased with the results - but it did take longer that I would have liked to figure it out.  In fact, the insufficient documentation is the only real criticism I have and the only reason I did not give it five stars.

review_headline: Read this for a real review
review_body: I have an original galaxy tab and decided to download this app since it is free so that I could test it and not give bs review based upon what everyone else was saying.  I often have to use the built in Android memory manager so that I can run more graphics intensive games, e.g. Plants vs Zombies and it is a hassle, so I would like an app to do it for me.  The problem is though, that most of these apps consume more resources then they free up.  That is certainly true with this app also.  For comparison purposes I first used the built in memory manager to exit all apps and then selected the ram tab to clear available ram.  I usually sit at about 348 MB before I clear the ram and afterwards typically sit at anywhere between 270 and 303 MB.  Anyhow, after I ran the ram cleaner I had 302 MB ram used.  I then ran the quick boost from this app and recovered a whopping 319 bytes...BYTES people!  The bottom line is that it just isn't worth it free or not when you have the same functionality built into Android.  My advice is to add the built in memory manager widget to your homescreen and just use that.

review_headline: Could use a few revisions, but this is a great app

Just review the app on the merits of its capabilities, people, and don't knock an app down because it does the same thing something else does.    That said, I recommend this for a lot of the people I work with.  It blows my mind how many people have one password for everything from their domain login to bank account access.  If one sight gets hacked, these people are going to be in a lot of trouble.    This app is great because it is stored on your phone, which most people (especially myself) have everywhere and is easier to grab then information in a dropbox account.     I do think the $5 is a little steep, or at a minimum include the ability to perform a desktop sync (that costs extra). This ap loads at startup and runs in the background all the time. It is a comparatively large ap (one of the biggest of the 50 odd aps I have on my tablet) and could cause problems for people with low ram or a slow processor. If you use it all the time, if it is one of the primary uses of your device then maybe that's OK (i.e. it isn't taking resources from something else).

Even so, it is something to be aware of. I stripped it off my tablet after 2 days because I grew tired of having to shut it down whenever I turned on my device... and wanted to use it for something else (and I have about the fastest processor available now on mobile devices), and a lot of ram. It is not a problem unless I am running another program which needs a lot of memory, but why have a memory hog running in the background? This service is not that much more convenient then others, not enough to where I think it is worth the amount of (disk) space it demands, or the memory load. Add to that what is effectively spyware (why would it be running in the background if it is not monitoring & reporting as you agreed to allow when you installed it). Personally I do not think the package is worth what it costs in terms of system lag... but that is a personal thing. If you do a lot of uploading and this service is your primary means of sharing pictures then it could be worth it to you. If your system is suddenly laggy, use something like taskill to turn it off.

I love word games, and this one is one of my favorite for the Android.

This is a lot like [[ASIN:B00000IWCZ Boggle]], on a 5x5 grid, except when you pick a word, then the letters go away. It also has a few special cubes that sometimes appear, like a ? cube, which you can use for any letter, and an orange shaded letter which doubles your score.

You get 2 minutes per round, and as soon as you get enough points, then the timer resets for that round, and you move to the next round, which also gets 2 minutes, uses the same board, and requires a few more points for completion. The letters carry over from round to round, so it makes it a fun challenge to try to use the hard letters first so you can score big letters later.

Pros:
+Very fun
+324 KB on my phone
+Can be moved to SD card (Appstore moved this automatically for me)
+You get exponentially higher scores, the more letters you play
+Combines the Q into QU, so q's are always easy to play
+Has a great dictionary, with all the crazy Scrabble words, like QUA, JEE, and ZEE

Cons:
-Probably a little too easy. Games for me last about 10 to 20 minutes before I \\"die\\", so you probably won't play a quick game of this.
-Only one mode of game play, even though this mode is very fun
-Small onscreen advertisements, but they're out of the way and don't interrupt game play, so they're okay

review_headline: Addicting until you beat the game
review_body: Bought this game by accident but ended up playing for over an hour.  The concept is simple, and the game is repetitive. Swipe your fingers across the screen to slash fruit. Don't slash the bombs.  There are three modes - classic (game ends once you miss 3 fruit or slash a bomb), zen (no bombs, 90s time limit), and arcade (bombs deduct points, special bananas enhance the game in different ways, 60s time limit).  As you play, you can unlock different blades (different visual effects as you slash fruit) and backgrounds.   I liked the graphics and found the game addicting. I kept playing until I unlocked all the blades and backgrounds. However, by the time I unlocked them all, I got bored and stopped wanting to play.

review_headline: And I'm not even a tower defense fan
review_body:
I couldn't tell you why I downloaded the free version of this game since I'm not a tower defense fan at *all*, but I became immediately hooked. Killing zombies with chain guns? Bring it! I then had to upgrade to the paid version (Gold), and I haven't regretted it, except for the sleep I lose at night playing.

It's pretty easy to learn and the gameplay is well-balanced - no unreasonable crushing defeats or easy victories. The graphics are decent, and the sound effects are good, although they can become a bit annoying when 8 or 10 chain guns are going off at the same time. Fortunately you have the ability to turn music and sound effects on or off.

The only complaint I really have is the maps are larger than my screen (HTC Thunderbolt), which means I need to scroll around to see everything. This is simply annoying until a stream of zombies sneaks by on a path you didn't see, and then it makes you want to throw you phone. Don't say I didn't warn you.
